To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sky brightness in the zenith during the totality of the 12 November 1986 eclipse at Bage, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, was 2.3 x 10 to the minus 5th power watts/meter squared/nanometer, and the spectral distribution of this brightness, as well as that during the partial phases, was similar to that of the moon.
The zenith sky intensity during totality was 1.2% of the solar intensity at the wavelength 550 nm.
The zenith sky intensity and the spectral distribution of the light scattered by the atmosphere during a total solar eclipse are functions of the altitude, the latitude, and the terrain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the measurement of the spectral distribution of the sky radiance during the total solar eclipse of November 12, 1966.
the study of the physical processes that control the chemical composition of the atmosphere.
the measurement of the spectral distribution and intensity of the solar eclipse light at the zenith.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, at least in this eclipse, the sky was not a good source of radiation during totality, except possibly at very short wavelengths.
, in the spectral region 0.3-1.0 microns, the zenith sky intensity is reduced by about 1/3 during totality.
, during a total solar eclipse, the zenith sky brightness is not greatly reduced and that the spectrum of the sky is not appreciably changed from the normal spectrum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, at least for the conditions prevailing during our observations, the sky intensity and spectral changes were not significantly different for the three sites and were not significantly different at the two sites where measurements were made during totality.
there was a general agreement between the various measurements, but that the changes were more marked at the higher altitudes and over the ocean than over the land.
the zenith sky intensity during totality is a function of height above the surface, with a minimum value of 0.1 to 0.2 of the normal intensity at about 10 km.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sky intensity during the eclipse is very sensitive to the terrain and that the spectral distribution of the sky radiation is also very sensitive to the altitude and terrain.
the sky is not black, and the spectral distribution of the sky radiation during totality is not the same as the distribution of the radiation from a blackbody at 2.7 K, as is commonly believed.
the spectral distribution of the light from the sky during totality is a function of the terrain and height of the observer.
